newsitem.title: USA: Sagan's last article focuses on greenhouse effect.
newsitem.headline: Sagan's last article focuses on greenhouse effect.

text.p: The late Carl Sagan, a premier populariser of the mysteries of astronomy, theorised in a newly published article that ammonia and methane kept the infant Earth and Mars warm enough to foster life.

The article in Friday's edition of the journal Science revisits a 25-year-old theory of Sagan's that the early atmospheres of Earth and Mars were loaded with so-called greenhouse gases that raised the surface temperatures enough to provide for liquid water -- seen as a requirement for life.
In the Science article Sagan adds methane to the mix that was needed in the formation of Earth, and possibly Mars.

Sagan, listed as the first author of the article, died of pneumonia on Dec. 20 at age 62. Co-author Christopher Chyba of the University of Tucson said this was probably the last article on which Sagan would be the first author, though Sagan may have contributed to others to be published later.

Sagan postulated 25 years ago that the greenhouse warming effect was needed because in the early days of Earth and Mars, about 4.5 billion years ago, the sun was much fainter than it is now and consequently could not raise temperatures on these two planets above freezing on its own.
In a 1972 article, Sagan dubbed this "the early faint sun paradox" and guessed that ammonia, a powerful greenhouse gas, was present on Earth and possibly on Mars.

The problem with that theory, Chyba said in a telephone interview, is that ammonia is destroyed by ultraviolet sunlight and would have been totally dissipated in a million years, an eyeblink in the context of cosmological time.
Since Sagan's earlier article, some scientists have suggested that the greenhouse effect was caused by carbon dioxide, but the new article suggested another possibility.

Sagan and Chyba said that another compound, methane, might have formed a protective smog layer that would filter out ultraviolet light so that the ammonia could survive to warm the early Earth. The same chemistry might also apply on Mars.
In this scenario, the ammonia would last about 500 million years, Chyba said, "and that's what you need to keep early Earth toasty, to keep it above freezing for the origins of life and so on."
The methane connection may have been sparked by Sagan's investigations of Titan, one of Saturn's moons, which has a similar methane smog layer, Chyba said.

The article was largely complete before Sagan's death, but Chyba made final changes later in response to editors' comments. A related article in Science by Jim Kasting of Pennsylvania State University was supportive, saying, "It seems likely that his (Sagan's) excellent scientific intuition will once again be found to be correct."
Chyba said this article should be viewed as a jumping-off point. "The way to view this paper is as a provocative suggestion that's going to lead to more detailed work," he said.
Sagan used books and television to convey the cosmos to ordinary people, winning the Pulitzer Prize in 1978 for "Dragons of Eden," a book that explored human intelligence.

He was perhaps best known for for "Cosmos," the award-winning 1980 television series and companion book on the workings of the universe, which was the most popular in the history of public television and was seen by some 500 million people.
